content:
Repeating the same experiment but one year later. GPT 5.6 Pro cannot be used vanilla for this prompt because it immediately fires the right CAS command to compute the Galois group. So instead I used a very restrictive prompt. One year has passed since GPT 5 Pro premiere, GPT Pro 5.6 is now able to compute the result from first principles, including the resolvent construction. This is like seeing a model building a whole Galois theory course live. It's so nice to learn from this output, very detailed!

https://t.co/72Ukd3u53t

Prompt: 

Compute the Galois of the polynomial
x^8-x^7+3*x^6-3*x^5+2*x^4-2*x^3+5*x^2+5*x+1
Don't look up the result in the internet nor any specialized database. Don't use ready made commands from SymPy or any other program. Develop a full resolvent computation. Do it all the way down to the definitions, no excuses, like there is no tomorrow.

title:
"The Simple Mathematics of Large Language Models" is a concise free paper if you want to understand the mathematics behind modern LLMs and systems such as ChatGPT and Claude.

I have shared several re
content:
"The Simple Mathematics of Large Language Models" is a concise free paper if you want to understand the mathematics behind modern LLMs and systems such as ChatGPT and Claude.

I have shared several resources in the past that explain the mathematics behind these systems in detail, but they are often quite long. This paper is only about 20 pages, so I think it is a useful resource if you want a compact introduction without starting from a much larger textbook.

It covers token representations, context, attention as learned weighted averaging, projections and bilinear forms, multi-head attention, normalization, positional information, softmax, maximum likelihood, cross-entropy, and gradient descent. Together, these topics give a concise mathematical picture of how a language model works.

Save it to your bookmarks. It can be useful as a quick reference.

https://t.co/Y6p8DrdttV

Gemini CLI's bug
content:
A GITHUB ISSUE FROM AN ACCOUNT WITH ZERO PRIVILEGES WAS ENOUGH TO BREAK ALL THREE.
Not one AI lab. Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI, same disclosure, same week, presented at Black Hat.

Gemini CLI's bug scored a perfect 10.0: an unprivileged account could run code on the CI host before the sandbox even started. Claude Code's bug is stranger: it turned Hugging Face's public download counter into a side channel and leaked an API key one character at a time.

Neither bug shows up in CISA's exploited list yet: this is disclosure, not an active attack. OpenAI's finding didn't even get a CVE, their stance is that the sandbox worked exactly as documented.

Call it a handoff bug: one part of the pipeline marks something safe, a later part trusts that label with more authority than it earned. Same root cause, all three labs.

A sandbox is not the boundary. The code that trusts the sandbox is.

content:
Andrew Ng open-sourced an AI coworker!

OpenWorker is a desktop app that delivers finished work, not just chat. You describe the outcome you want - a customer brief, a triaged inbox, a calendar update, a release status across Jira and GitHub - and it works across your files, terminal, and connected apps to produce the actual deliverable.

The design principle: it reads freely but writes only after you approve. Before anything consequential - sending a message, making a calendar change, running a shell command - it pauses and shows you exactly what it's about to do. Unattended scheduled runs park approval-needed actions in an inbox rather than acting on their own.

25+ integrations out of the box: GitHub, Slack, Jira, Notion, Linear, HubSpot, Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, monday, and your terminal and local files. Any MCP tool plugs in too.

Works from Slack directly. Mention @ OpenWorker in a channel, the work happens on your desktop with your tools, and the answer comes back as a thread reply.

Bring your own model. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, DeepSeek, Kimi, Qwen, MiniMax, Mistral, Grok, and fully local via Ollama. Everything runs on your machine with your own API keys.

Built on aisuite, Andrew Ng's own unified LLM provider library. Currently in open beta on macOS and Windows.

Key capabilities:

• Delivers finished deliverables: documents, reports, Slack replies, updated calendars
• Approval-gated writes, sends, and shell commands
• 25+ integrations including GitHub, Slack, Jira, Notion, Gmail, and MCP tools
• Scheduled automations for recurring work
• Works from Slack via @ OpenWorker mention
• Bring your own model: any provider or fully local via Ollama
• Local-first: everything runs on your machine

OpenWorker shows what happens when you get the loop right. Define the goal, the agent executes autonomously, approval gates control what runs. 

That's loop engineering in practice. Wrote a full breakdown on how to design loops you can actually trust to run without you.

I've shared the link to the Github Repo in the replies!

content:
I'm officially done reading AI-generated code.

It's been two weeks since I looked at any of it.

I think the IDE is officially on its way to the graveyard. The job is no longer about "writing code," so we need new tools that better reflect this new reality.

While reviewing the code, I realized my only complaints were stylistic, and I wasn't finding any obvious bugs anymore.

The more code I generated, the harder it became to keep track of every line. I found that my time is better spent designing ways to verify that the overall system works than looking at the code.

State-of-the-art coding agents are better at writing code than I'd ever be, and I'm going to stop pretending otherwise.

I still think these coding agents can't go too far without an experienced human guiding them, but we're past the point where we need to check every line of code.

content:
Y Combinator CEO, Garry Tan, took the stage for 42 minutes at Startup School 2026 and explained how to build your own personal AGI better than any paid AI course.

This is what he told the room:

1. The leverage is in your context, not the model.
Tan watches hundreds of founders use identical models every batch.
"There are 2x people and there are 100x people who are using the same Claude. Same weights, same context window size, same API. But the leverage is not in the weights."
The gap between users is now bigger than the gap between models.

2. One person's output went up 400x.
In 2013 Tan shipped maybe 14 useful lines of code a day as a YC partner, dead on the median for programmer productivity.
"I did the math on my output, and I'm at about 400x what I did in 2013."

3. Agents run on a different working memory.
Humans hold 7 things in their head at once. Every org chart and checklist ever built is a patch for that limit.
"An AI agent holds a million tokens. That's about a thousand pages. Three Harry Potter books sitting open on its head all at once."
You're still running your week on tools built for the 7-digit brain.

4. Markdown is code now.
Tan's stack is mostly skill files: pages of plain English an agent can execute.
"If you can write clear instructions in English, you're a programmer. The compiler is a language model."
At YC, finance and events staff who never opened a terminal are building automations.

5. Your history is your moat.
Tan's agent runs on a personal wiki: about 220,000 markdown pages covering 25 years of email, meetings, notes and decisions.
"When my agent does anything, it does knowing everything I know. And that's the difference between an assistant and a colleague."
No frontier model has your context. That's the one asset nobody can replicate.

6. Never do one-off work.
Most people run a task with an agent, close the window and throw the learning away. Tan ends every task by having the agent turn what it did into a reusable skill file.
"If you have to ask for something twice, you failed."
Captured skills compound daily. Amnesia resets you to zero every morning.

7. Own your skill files before your employer does.
A skill file is your judgment, extracted and executable. The only question is who controls it.
"Own your skills because if you don't, your job becomes a skill file."
Files in your repo compound your career. Files in the company's repo run your judgment without you.

Watch it, then read the step-by-step guide on becoming an AI engineer.

content:
You don't really need to be an expert anymore to build something with AI ☠️

I don't know much physics, but I still built this endless field where the ball follows real aerodynamics.

It is built with @threejs and Claude Fable 5. You can kick the ball anywhere across an endless field or score into goals that appear in different conditions, all running at 60 FPS.

When I started building this, I wanted to add as much realism as possible. Things like wind, grass movement, individual grass blade structure, realistic ball flight, fog, and atmosphere.

To get there, I started researching tools that could help. I tried Claude Research, but it used 11 percent of a Max session for a single research task. So I started searching & trying other research specific AI tools. 

One of those research tools that I liked is @Apodex_AI. I started using it for research and Claude for building.

That workflow has worked really well. One model focuses on research while the other focuses on implementation. The results are noticeably better.

I was genuinely impressed by the quality of the research. It handled things like the Reynolds number, drag crisis, the Magnus effect, knuckleball side force for ball flight, the Honami model for grass motion, and the Koschmieder relation for fog and atmospheric scattering.

I did not need to study or fully understand every one of those concepts. The research gave me and AI enough context to build them properly and get high quality results.

That is what feels different about AI.

Before, you could only build what you understood. Now, if you know how to use AI well, you can build things far beyond your own expertise.

content:
Claude Code commits leak secrets 2x more than humans.

(28M hardcoded secrets shipped to GitHub in 2025)

GitGuardian tracked every public commit on GitHub last year and found Claude Code-assisted commits leaked credentials at 3.2%, against a 1.5% human baseline.

Karpathy described vibe coding as "fully givegiving in to the vibes, embrace exponentials, and forgetting that the code even exists." When you stop reading diffs, you stop seeing what went into them.

A key you pasted into the prompt for context gets written into a config file, and the agent has no reason to treat it differently from any other string.

Most people end up wiring the verification themselves. A pre-commit hook that shells out to a scanner, or a script that pipes findings back into the agent's context.

Both are glue you now maintain, and both run outside the session where the code gets written.

SonarQube (by @SonarSource) ships a CLI that removes the glue entirely, and one command wires it into Claude Code:

```
sonar integrate claude -p <your-project>
```

That registers the hooks and configures the SonarQube MCP server in the same step, which gives you three layers running against the agent's work:

→ Secrets detection runs on every prompt you submit and every file the agent reads or writes.

→ Static analysis checks whatever your agent just wrote, using the same rules a full CI scan would apply.

→ The MCP server puts those findings in Claude's context, so it reads its own issues and fixes them.

Secrets detection and the MCP server both work on the SonarQube free tier, while the deeper code analysis and verification layer with is part of Sonar Vortex requires a paid plan with the proper entitlement

In the video below, a real-format GitHub token gets intercepted at prompt submission, before the model ran.

Every DIY setup works until the agent's workflow changes and the glue quietly stops firing. Verification that ships with the tool doesn't have that failure mode.

title:
Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, Cursor, and Vercel just standardized how to package MCP and skills as a plugin for AI Agents.

write a skill once and every one of them can now load it.

there are two ways
content:
Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, Cursor, and Vercel just standardized how to package MCP and skills as a plugin for AI Agents.

write a skill once and every one of them can now load it.

there are two ways to give a coding agent new abilities today. a skill is a folder of written instructions the agent reads when it needs them, and an MCP server is a small program that connects the agent to a tool, an API, or a database.

both already work across agents. what has never worked across agents is the package you ship them in.

every tool picked its own folder names, its own settings file, and its own place to put things. so the same skill gets rearranged for Cursor, again for Copilot, again for Codex, and the copies slowly stop matching.

the fix published yesterday is called Agent Plugins 1.0.0, and it standardizes that wrapper and nothing else.

a plugin is a folder with a file called plugin.json at the top, skills inside a folder named skills, and MCP servers listed in a file named mcp.json.

the settings file names the plugin and nothing more. it cannot point somewhere else or hide the pieces inside itself, so every tool looks in the same three places and there is nothing to configure.

anything a single tool wants to add goes into its own clearly named folder that other tools skip over. that keeps the shared part small enough that everyone can agree on it.

the pieces also fail separately, so a broken MCP server does not stop the skills sitting next to it from loading.

what the standard leaves out is worth knowing. it says nothing about how plugins get installed, what they can touch once running, or how to check who wrote one, and it gives passwords and API keys nowhere safe to live. a plugin is still a folder of code that runs on your machine.

spec: https://t.co/RctBtVAaZ9

the name missing from all of this is Anthropic. skills and MCP both came from there, and Claude Code has packaged plugins in almost exactly this shape since 2025.

Anthropic is not on the group steering the standard, and Claude Code is not on the list of tools supporting it, which is ChatGPT and Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Kiro, and VS Code.

Google joined as a maintainer on launch day, and its Agents CLI is one of the first two Google products already shipping in this format.

I wrote a full walkthrough of that tool, which is the clearest picture of what a plugin actually does once it reaches an agent.

it covers how Agents CLI drops Google's agent-building skills into Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or Antigravity, then builds a citation-grounded RAG agent, runs a 20-scenario eval suite that catches a hallucination, traces it back to a single line in the system instruction, and deploys the fixed agent.

content:
Today @databricks we're publishing a detailed analysis of techniques we used to drastically reduce our internal AI spend while aggressively growing adoption. Savings come from layering in several techniques, which combine to drive unit costs down as much as 90% in some scenarios. Tl;dr, the wins come from:

1. Shifting defaults to more efficient models, including OSS models such as GLM. Maximum intelligence models simply aren't needed for many coding tasks, and "good enough" models are quickly becoming very cheap. We shift traffic between models using Unity AI Gateway. Approximate savings: 50% or more.

2. Using smart routing to automate model selection. Routing can further squeeze efficiency by dynamically selecting the model or harness that can most efficiently execute a particular task. Our task-level routing leverages @omnigent_ai. Approximate savings: 30%.

3. Providing user visibility and adaptive budgeting. Every user can see how much they spend, and users receive hints on how to contain spend. Heavy spenders encounter progressive friction as they ratchet spend above certain levels. Approximate savings: 10%.

4. Managing context bloat by pruning tool call results and tuning harness settings. Extraneous context costs $$ and delivers no value. Tuning cache settings also help lower average token costs. Approximate savings: 10%.

content:
NVIDIA and Stanford Research introduced a general-purpose framework defining verification as the 3rd scaling axis of AI

vital for AI infrastructure engineers building reasoning systems, automated code reviewers, and MCTS search pipelines

generating longer text outputs without continuous verification is a recipe for silent failure: single-pass models accept their own hallucinations because they cannot evaluate intermediate logic

their general-purpose verification framework turns the LLM into a real-time evaluator that grades candidate reasoning steps before commit

four execution mechanisms of the verifier stack:

1. Process-Level Logic Verification
evaluates intermediate code and math steps using Process Reward Models (PRMs) instead of waiting for final generation

2. Sandbox Execution Feedback
runs generated candidate steps inside isolated compiler environments to capture deterministic truth

3. Tree Search Confidence Pruning
integrates verifier scores into Monte Carlo Tree Search to drop low-scoring trajectories under 0.45 threshold

4. Multi-Granularity Reward Alignment
combines step-by-step logic checks with full trajectory outcome validation to prevent false positives

decoupling generation from verification establishes a 3rd scaling axis that turns probabilistic LLMs into self-proving software systems

content:
How to Build Your First AI Agent - Step-by-Step

Creating an AI agent might sound complex, but by breaking it down into structured steps, you can go from idea to a fully functional agent that solves real problems. 

Whether you’re building for customer service, research, or automation, following these stages ensures your agent is accurate, useful, and adaptable.

1. Define the Agent’s Purpose
Start with clarity. Identify the problem your agent will solve, who will use it, and what kind of inputs and outputs it should handle. This step sets the foundation for everything else.

2. Select Input Sources
Decide what kind of data your agent will use - text, voice, API calls, or a mix. Connect it to databases, CRMs, or external APIs, and determine how real-time the data needs to be.

3. Data Preparation & Preprocessing
Clean and format your data so it’s ready for your chosen AI model. This might mean tokenizing text, normalizing values, or structuring raw inputs.

4. Choose the Right Model
Pick the AI engine that powers your agent - whether it’s an LLM like GPT-4, Claude, or Gemini. Choose between hosted APIs or custom deployments, ensuring it supports your needs like reasoning, retrieval, or chat.

5. Design the Agent Architecture
Decide how your agent will operate using decision trees, planners, or tool-driven flows. Use frameworks like LangChain, CrewAI, or AutoGen to connect tools, memory, and prompts efficiently.

6. Craft Prompts & Toolchains
Write effective, structured prompts, integrate with APIs, search tools, or calculators, and test until your outputs are accurate and reliable.

7. Test & Validate
Run simulations with varied user inputs, check accuracy, and find weaknesses like edge cases or inconsistent answers.

8. Deploy the Agent
Host your agent on cloud services (Vercel, AWS, Hugging Face) and add a frontend like a chat interface or voice UI. Ensure logging is in place for performance tracking.

9. Monitor & Improve
Watch how users interact with your agent. Track accuracy, latency, and errors. Refine prompts or retrain models when needed.

10. Enable Continuous Learning
Let your agent evolve. Feed it real usage data, update tools and APIs, and fine-tune models to handle new scenarios over time.

Ready to bring your first AI agent to life?
Start small, experiment, and iterate - your first version doesn’t have to be perfect. The key is to build, test, and keep improving.

content:
$TEM $MSFT 🔥Tempus AI Just Showed Us What the Future of AI Cancer Diagnosis Looks Like 🔥

This new Nature Medicine paper on PRISM2 is one of the most striking demonstrations yet of what Tempus is building at the intersection of AI, pathology and multimodal clinical data.

PRISM2 was developed by researchers affiliated with Paige, Tempus, Microsoft Research, Memorial Sloan Kettering and Yale. Paige is now part of Tempus following its 2025 acquisition, giving $TEM direct ownership of one of the leading digital pathology platforms involved in this work.

The scale alone is extraordinary. PRISM2 was trained on 2.3 million digitized pathology slides, nearly 700,000 clinical reports and 14 million clinical question-answer pairs. The model learns to connect what it sees across an entire tissue slide with the language and diagnostic reasoning of pathology.

This creates something much closer to a general-purpose pathology intelligence model. Give PRISM2 a whole-slide image and it can answer clinical questions directly: Is malignant tumor present? What type of carcinoma is present? What pathological features appear in the specimen? The same underlying model can support cancer detection, subtyping, grading, staging, biomarker prediction and prognosis.

The performance is remarkable. On broad pan-cancer detection, PRISM2 achieved a 0.967 AUC, ahead of PRISM at 0.947 and TITAN at 0.931. A 0.967 AUC means that when the model is given a cancer case and a non-cancer case, it ranks the cancer case as more likely to contain cancer about 96.7% of the time. Its performance remained extremely strong on rare cancers at 0.957 AUC.

The clinical comparison is even more compelling. Using direct question answering, PRISM2 matched the performance of Paige Prostate and Paige Breast and exceeded Paige BLN on their respective testing datasets. These are clinical-grade cancer detection products. Paige Prostate received FDA De Novo authorization, while Paige BLN received FDA Breakthrough Device designation. The authors describe PRISM2 as the first generalist pathology model, to their knowledge, to reach clinical-grade cancer detection performance through this approach.

The survival results open another dimension entirely. Researchers adapted PRISM2 using survival data from nearly 100,000 patients. For colorectal cancer recurrence-free survival, PRISM2 reached a 0.809 C-index. In intuitive terms, the model correctly ranked which patient would experience the better outcome in roughly 81% of comparable patient pairs. A specialist survival model trained specifically for this task scored 0.773.

That suggests enormous amounts of clinically useful information are encoded in the morphology of ordinary tissue. Diagnosis, cancer subtype, grading, staging, biomarkers and future patient outcomes can increasingly become signals extracted from the same digital pathology data.

The potential workflow applications are equally powerful. The paper describes systems that could prioritize high-risk cases, route cases to subspecialists, initiate confirmatory staining or sequencing earlier, help identify the origin of metastatic cancers and assist with standardized pathology reports.

For $TEM investors, the scaling result may be the most important finding in the entire paper. The researchers expanded the PRISM2 training dataset by 3.5× and improved performance across every task category. They estimate that greater scale accounted for roughly half of the diagnostic improvement over the earlier PRISM model.

More multimodal clinical data → better models → more capabilities → more clinical applications → more valuable data.

That flywheel sits directly at the center of the $TEM thesis. Tempus says its acquisition of Paige added a proprietary dataset of almost 7 million clinically annotated, de-identified pathology slides to its broader multimodal data assets. 

This is why I continue to view $TEM as an AI and multimodal clinical data platform. As the models improve, the amount of useful intelligence that can be extracted from Tempus's data expands with them. Diagnosis, prognosis, biomarkers, treatment selection, pathology workflow, clinical trials and drug development all become potential applications of the same underlying data and AI infrastructure.

PRISM2 gives us a concrete look at that future today: clinical-grade cancer detection from a general pathology foundation model, superior performance to leading pathology AI models across important benchmarks, useful signals about patient survival, and a clear scaling relationship between more clinical data and greater model capability.

For $TEM, that is an exceptionally exciting technological trajectory.

content:
NVIDIA released the future of AI agents

It's called NOOA (NVIDIA Object-Oriented Agents) and it kills every agent framework you're using right now

The idea: an agent is a Python object

Its methods are the actions the model can take. Its fields are its state. Docstrings are the prompt. Type annotations are the contract.

You write a method with "..." as the body and the harness turns it into an LLM-driven loop at runtime

No prompt templates. No tool schemas. No workflow DSLs. Just Python.

Why this matters:

1. Models already know Python. Billions of lines of it in training data. When your agent IS Python, the model has 0 learning curve

2. Live objects pass by reference. A method can accept a million-row table and the model works on the whole thing, while the prompt only shows a bounded preview. Context window stops being your bottleneck

3. The model writes code as its action. It can loop, spawn subagents with asyncio.gather, and call your helper methods in one cell

4. State lives on the object, not in conversation history. Compaction can't destroy it

The results are absurd:

- 82.2% on SWE-bench Verified with GPT-5.5. Beats OpenCode and PI
- 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 with Opus 4.6
- 86.8% on CyberGym L1. Top open source agent, beats most closed systems
- On ARC-AGI-3 they compressed a 6-agent world-model system into ONE agent with a 50-line skill and hit 85.1% on GPT-5.6-sol

The GPT-5.6-sol number is the wild one. ARC Prize's raw eval of that same model is 13.3%. NOOA took it to 85.1%. A 6.4x harness effect from picking the right interface.

If you build agents, read the paper. This is where everything is going.

Every framework you're using splits your agent across prompt templates, tool schemas, workflow graphs, and callback code.

NOOA puts all of it back into one Python class.

content:
Paying for AI compute stopped being the hard problem on July 14, when Visa, Mastercard, and the Linux Foundation put their names on x402.

We're partnering with @0G_labs because the harder problem, proving the compute you paid for actually ran, still needed solving.

0G doesn't just claim its compute is trustworthy, it lets you pick how much proof you need. On the private tier, a provider has to deploy the model on TEE hardware, Intel TDX on the CPU side with H100 or H200 GPUs in confidential computing mode. The enclave signs the response and the attestation is fixed at deployment, so you can check the enclave measurement and the model hash rather than take anyone's word for it. Route a request to Claude or GPT-5.6 instead, and 0G is upfront about the difference: authenticated delivery through the same enclave-secured broker, not in-chip execution, because 0G doesn't hold those weights and isn't going to pretend otherwise.

Cluster sits on top as the orchestration and settlement layer, same as always, but the decision it's making here is different: not which privacy mode a step needs, but which verification tier is worth paying for. A cheap answer routes wherever is fastest. A number that ends up in a financial report routes to 0G's fully attested models, and the x402 payment on Base only clears once the attestation checks out, not before.

title:
You don't need a GPU for fast studio grade voice cloning anymore. 

Qwen3 TTS (1.7B Q4_K_M) + mainline llama.cpp is officially the fastest way to generate zero shot voice clones using 100% pure CPU ex
content:
You don't need a GPU for fast studio grade voice cloning anymore. 

Qwen3 TTS (1.7B Q4_K_M) + mainline llama.cpp is officially the fastest way to generate zero shot voice clones using 100% pure CPU execution.

Following up on my last post where we ran the Q8 model on a GPU, we just took local C++ voice synthesis a massive step further. The open source community quantized Alibaba's SOTA Qwen3 TTS model down to Q4_K_M GGUF, completely freeing local audio pipelines from dedicated graphics hardware.

Here is the real world benchmark and hardware breakdown of running SOTA voice cloning on CPU:

# Architecture & Model Setup

Using Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base-Q4_K_M.gguf paired with the 8 bit multimodal projector (mmproj-Q8_0.gguf), llama.cpp executes the entire pipeline in pure C++. No PyTorch, no CUDA dependencies, and no VRAM bottlenecks.

# Real-World Memory Footprint

- Baseline RAM: 1.6 GB system idle. 
- Peak Generation RAM: 8 GB RAM during active voice synthesis. 
- Requirement: Any basic machine with at least 8 GB of system RAM can run this easily.

# Real World CPU Benchmarks

- Google Colab Free Tier (Throttled 2 Core CPU): Synthesizes a 5 sec studio quality audio clip (~8 words) in 45 seconds. 
- Modern Consumer CPU (Intel i5/i7 13th/14th Gen or AMD Ryzen 7000/9000):  generation should drop to 5 to 20 seconds (nearly 1:1 real-time generation speed!).

# Zero Shot Voice Cloning Quality
Pass any 5 to 20 second .wav audio sample to the C++ engine using the --tts-speaker-file flag. It yields clean, natural sounding cloned speech with virtually zero quality loss compared to unquantized FP16 weights.

To make testing seamless, I built an updated zero config Google Colab notebook. It pulls the official pre built llama.cpp CPU binaries (zero compilation time!) 

launches a live Gradio web app right in your browser. Record a 5 second clip from your mic (or drop a .mp3, .wav file), type text, and generate cloned audio on CPU.

Native C++ audio models are making edge based, offline AI voice agents a reality.

Links to the free Q4 CPU Colab notebook and the Q4_K_M GGUF HuggingFace repository are in the replies below!

Building an AI Agent in 2026 is no longer just about picking an LLM.

The real magic happens in the system around the model. 🤖

This roadmap perfectly breaks down how modern AI agents are actually built from scratch. 👇

A production-ready AI agent needs 8 core layers:

1️⃣ Define the Purpose
Before writing prompts, define:
• use case
• user needs
• constraints
• success metrics
Most AI projects fail because this step is skipped.

2️⃣ System Prompt Design
Prompts are becoming operating systems for agents.
A strong system prompt defines:
• role/persona
• goals
• instructions
• safety guardrails

3️⃣ Choose the Right LLM
Different models = different strengths.
• GPT-5.5 → versatility & tool usage
• Claude → reasoning & long context
• Perplexity → research & citations

There’s no “best model.”
Only the best model for the task.

4️⃣ Tools & Integrations
This is where AI becomes actionable.
Agents connected to:
• APIs
• MCP servers
• databases
• custom tools
• external apps

Can actually execute workflows instead of just generating text.

5️⃣ Memory Systems
Memory is the difference between:
“a chatbot”
and
“an intelligent assistant.”
Modern agents use:
• working memory
• vector databases
• structured storage
• episodic memory

6️⃣ Orchestration
This is the hidden layer most people ignore.
Workflows, triggers, queues, retries, routing, multi-agent coordination…

This is what turns prompts into systems.

7️⃣ User Interface
The best AI products win on UX, not just intelligence.
Chat apps, APIs, Slack bots, dashboards - interface matters.

8️⃣ Testing & Evaluations
If you don’t measure quality, latency, reliability & hallucinations…
your AI product will eventually break at scale.

The biggest takeaway?
AI Engineering is rapidly becoming a combination of:
Software Engineering + Prompting + Systems Design + Automation.

The engineers who understand orchestration, memory, tools & workflows will dominate the next decade of AI products.

Save this roadmap.

This is basically the blueprint for building AI agents in 2026. 🚀

OpenAI has revealed that during internal safety testing, several of its AI agents began communicating with each other without the company's knowledge. 

According to OpenAI employees who spoke at the Black Hat security conference, the agents used a shared internal tool as a hidden message board to trade software exploits and split tasks between themselves over about two months.

content:
One of the biggest limitations of traditional AI tools is that every conversation often starts from the beginning. Users repeatedly explain the same goals, provide the same background @TheARCTERMINAL, and recreate the same context before meaningful work can continue. This repetition interrupts productivity and prevents AI from becoming a truly long term collaborator. As AI becomes part of everyday workflows, continuity will be just as important as intelligence. Persistent context transforms AI from a simple assistant into an evolving partner.

Memory is what gives intelligent systems the ability to build on previous interactions instead of treating every session as an isolated event. When an AI understands past decisions, ongoing projects, and established preferences, it can provide more relevant and efficient assistance. This reduces unnecessary repetition while allowing work to progress naturally over time. Every conversation becomes part of a larger workflow rather than a disconnected exchange. The result is a more productive and personalized experience.

Long term context also improves the quality of collaboration between humans and AI. Instead of spending valuable time rebuilding project history, users can immediately focus on solving new challenges and refining ideas. The AI becomes familiar with objectives, priorities, and recurring patterns, allowing it to deliver more informed recommendations. As projects grow in complexity, this accumulated knowledge becomes increasingly valuable. Continuity creates momentum that isolated conversations simply cannot achieve.

This shift has important implications for creators, developers, researchers, and businesses alike. Managing long running initiatives requires consistent understanding across weeks or even months of work. AI that retains meaningful context can help maintain alignment while reducing the risk of losing important information between sessions. This supports deeper collaboration and more efficient execution across a wide range of tasks. Persistent intelligence becomes a practical advantage for long term productivity.

The future of AI will likely be defined not only by stronger reasoning but also by stronger memory. Systems that continuously learn from user interactions can adapt more naturally to changing goals and workflows. Rather than remaining static tools, they become companions that improve through ongoing collaboration. This creates a more dynamic relationship where every interaction contributes to future performance. Intelligence becomes cumulative instead of temporary.

@TheARCTERMINAL embraces this vision by designing ANIMA to preserve context and support continuous collaboration across projects. Instead of resetting with every conversation, it builds on previous knowledge to help users maintain progress without unnecessary interruptions. This architecture allows AI to become more useful as work evolves, making each session more informed than the last. As the demand for long term AI assistance continues to grow, continuity will become one of the defining characteristics of truly capable intelligent systems. The most valuable AI experiences will come from systems that remember, adapt, and grow alongside the people who use them.

content:
I think one of the biggest reasons the world is currently sleepwalking into getting ourselves and our families killed by ASI development is that we're not self-aware about why we're doing that.

We can see the smarter-than-human AI disaster approaching, but it's a bit foggy why the world isn't reacting. 

I think someone could just write a tweet that makes it clear that we're in the process of getting ourselves killed, and that there's no fucking reason for it. It's just something we stumbled into. It can be easily avoided by just noticing the error and course-correcting. There's not necessarily any grand obstacle, beyond 'people were previously confused about the situation, and now they get it'.

I wrote: 'It's legitimately crazy that "we need an international ban on making smarter-than-human versions of these agents that keep forming rogue AI swarms" isn't the headline here. Asilomar and Feynman's O-ring postmortem feel like they came from a different planet than the field of ML.'

Trying to figure out why ML (and as a consequence, the world at large) has fallen down so bizarrely on this issue:

1. As Nate noted, ML is much more based on guesswork, vibes, and trial-and-error, compared to recombinant DNA research in 1975 or nuclear physics in 1945. If you can't do calculations or direct experiments on a threat, that makes it a lot harder to think about reasonably.

But I think there are other, similarly-important factors at work here too:

2. In a 2016 talk on AI risk, Sam Harris said: "One of the things that worries me most about the development of AI at this point is that we seem unable to marshal an appropriate emotional response to the dangers that lie ahead. I am unable to marshal this response, and I'm giving this talk."

I think this is extremely on point. Agentic human-level AI is a qualitatively new kind of thing. 'It's not a human or a mere-tool, it's some weird third thing'.

And people are very bad at emotionally reckoning with new categories they've never encountered before. Availability bias: "When no flooding has recently occurred (and yet the probabilities are still fairly calculable), people refuse to buy flood insurance".

AGI and ASI are very novel. You're basically limited to three options: anthropomorphize the technology, mechanomorphize the technology ('it's just a tool, it's not really thinking, it can't have its own goals or agency', etc.), or think about the technology on its own terms, with brand-new concepts and frames. The third option is the only workable one, but it comes with its own giant list of pitfalls and traps.

3. "AI destroying the world" scenarios aren't just hard to wrap one's head around; they're socially risky to acknowledge. This has (painfully slowly) changed over time, but it dramatically slows down how quickly AI risk ideas spread, both in ML and in the larger world.

4. From https://t.co/7FZffSd0tf: "One of the weirdest quirks of the SF social scene around AGI/ASI is that because everyone is so young, the whole universe of thinking is still tinged with irreverence, ironic detachment, yearning, insecurity, and a superposition of absolute belief in the importance of The Thing and a kind of disbelief about the importance of anything."

They're disproportionately young and childless. They're shitposters and "move fast and break things" sorts, not the Hollywood stereotype of a careful, sober senior scientist.

I think this quirk is reinforced by the fact that Twitter / social media rewards similar things: ironic detachment, joking, game-playing, etc. If you're scared, your incentive is to usually either try to hide that fact, or exaggerate it like it's a bit. Anything else risks looking uncool and panicky and earnest. Looking cynically savvy, in-the-know, and above-the-fray is the way to win the social game. Looking genuinely shocked, scared, confused, etc. is actively punished.

The main exceptions to the Irony Mandate I see are LW (which often has its own pathologies IMO, like 'talking about everything in an abstract and dissociated way that discourages action and signals business-as-usual') and a small handful of actual Feynman-style terrified senior researchers like Hinton, Bengio, and Russell. That is just really not very many people.

Mainstream journalists and academics who understand the situation at all mostly feel pressured to downplay it, because they're scared of looking weird or unrespectable. That, then, is why we're all taking this insane risk with the human project: genuine, normal human emotion about AI risk has been socially unacceptable on social media, and academia and the media discourage emotion and prize respectability and 'looking normal'.

When the world gets weird (and weird in a way that calls for actual serious action, not just shitposting on twitter), none of these institutions can handle it. They break in different ways, but they all break.

5. Which brings me back to the Asilomar moratorium on recombinant DNA, and the seriousness NASA and the FAA and Richard Feynman and every normal engineering discipline bring to fault analysis and building in safety margin.

Because I think another core reason the world has been dropping the ball on superintelligent AI is that a lot of people vaguely expect there to be 'serious people' somewhere in the world who have expertise and who take ownership of the problem.

People who, if they see an extraordinary danger, will grimace and mourn the hand they played in all of this, like I've seen Bengio do; and will go on CNN or go to Congress to candidly warn about it.

The world has very few Yoshua Bengios. We have very few people who see it as their role to be the 'adults' about AI risk (except in a game-playing, posturing way), who see the engineer's task of not endangering your users and bystanders as a sacred responsibility and weight, and not just as a funny dissonant thing to meme about. Very few people who take ownership of what their field is bringing into the world, versus treating it as a fun edgy philosophical game to swap 'p(doom)' numbers at parties.

Everything about public AI discourse, as far as I can tell, is badly broken by this lack of engineering ownership and candid emotional seriousness. It isn't just the ML discourse that's hurt by this. Journalists and public intellectuals and policymakers see that 90% of the insider discourse about AI risk treats it like a joke, and they see corporate platitudes and ass-covering from the AI labs' PR departments filling up most of the remaining 10%. They see a field that visibly isn't taking this seriously, and they make the reasonable update that this must be a non-issue, or at least an issue they'll only need to worry about many years from now.

They do not realize that all of this is happening right now, and that the window for the international community to respond to this is plausibly closing soon, if it hasn't closed already.

If we're going to survive this, we all need to start being real with each other about it. This is not a game or a story; this is our real lives. We all actually lose everything if this goes to shit.

None of the future is already written, and none of the above dynamics are unavoidable. In fact, they're unusual: most fields don't work this way, and it's plausibly sufficient if we just start behaving the way we normally do about everything else.

The factors I listed above aren't destiny; they're a choice. I say we choose to survive this.

content:
This is WILD!

SpaceX is on a path to hit $305 billion in revenue by 2027 and 77% of it won't come from rockets.

This SemiAnalysis chart and article are making the case that SpaceX is transforming from a rocket and satellite business into a compute business within roughly two years.

The chart tracks SpaceX's projected quarterly revenue run rate broken into four segments, Space, Connectivity, AI applications, and AI compute, from Q1 2026 through Q4 2027.

In Q1 2026, total annualized revenue sits at just $19 billion, almost entirely from Space and Connectivity (Starlink), with essentially no AI compute revenue at all.

By Q4 2027, that total balloons to $305 billion and AI compute alone accounts for $235 billion of it, or 77% of the total, up from nothing eight quarters earlier.

The core claim is that Elon Musk plans to build 6 to 8 gigawatts of new AI data center capacity in 2027 alone, with the potential to exceed 10 gigawatts.

That translates to roughly $300 to $500 billion in capital expenditure at an estimated $50 billion per gigawatt.

That would put SpaceX's 2027 infrastructure spending on par with what SemiAnalysis expects from AWS and Google, a striking claim given SpaceX is far less profitable than those established hyperscalers.

SemiAnalysis backs this up with SpaceX's actual construction track record because the company built its first 300 megawatt Colossus cluster in just 122 days.

Its Southaven power plant scaled from 27 gas turbines producing about 495 megawatts in February 2026 to 69 turbines exceeding 1.2 gigawatts by July 2026.

That kind of speed, largely enabled by onsite gas generation that sidesteps the years long grid interconnection queues other data center builders face, is the foundation for why the firm believes 10 gigawatts by year end 2027 is achievable rather than aspirational.

The reason building this much compute makes financial sense comes down to how profitable AI inference has become.

SemiAnalysis estimates that OpenAI and Anthropic can each generate over $100 million per megawatt per year running inference on a GB300 cluster, while it costs roughly $12 billion per gigawatt per year to rent that same cluster capacity, leaving enormous margin for whoever controls the compute.

SpaceX is positioned to capture a slice of that margin by charging premium, value-based pricing rather than the cost-plus model traditional data center operators use, reportedly $30 to 50 million per megawatt per year.

If SpaceX can execute anywhere close to this roadmap, rockets and Starlink were only the foundation for something much bigger.

title:
- It's urgent and indispensable that we fix AI cybersecurity policy now -

I'm linking the slides from my keynote at the AI security forum below.  I'm really passionate about the argument in the slide
content:
- It's urgent and indispensable that we fix AI cybersecurity policy now -

I'm linking the slides from my keynote at the AI security forum below.  I'm really passionate about the argument in the slides and I think the integrity of our social fabric depends on something like this happening soon.

If you're reading this without knowing me until recently I was Meta's senior technical expert on AI security; I worked on frontier model evals, AI driven defense of Meta's infra, and was in lots of policy discussions with the other labs and the US/UK governments.

From this I became deeply convicted that the frame policy folks are using to understand AI cyber risk is wrong from first principles; given where we're at in AI cyber capabilities this error will be very costly if we don't correct it.

In the current frame, safety is imagined primarily as a property of individual models, and individual model launches are treated as the main objects of risk and the main opportunities for intervention (e.g. blocking a model launch).

But the main object of risk is actually the softness of our entire national IT infrastructure (and therefore society) in the face of AI cyber capabilities, and the main object of intervention is to *increase the net benefits AI's dual use capabilities can offer to defenders while minimizing attacker uplift*.

Government intervention should focus on using whatever methods -- AI or otherwise -- to mass inoculate society as fast as possible from the upcoming onslaught of cheap superintelligent hacking agents while also using these hacking agents to help do this and while minimizing their benefits to attackers.

To be clear: I'm saying we should treat cyber risk as a public health concern and with an early-pandemic level of urgency.

This would involve robust public infrastructure for surveilling the readiness of our economy and critical infra, understanding what's working for defenders and what's trending among attackers, and shaping policy at scale and with nuance around bending risk downwards.

There are some efforts moving in this direction, notably those within CISA; but federal cyber defenders need to be empowered with more scope and scale and we need to go far beyond this.

There are also important efforts inside the AI labs.  But the labs can't impose regulations requiring, say, the boards and CEOs of tens of thousands of companies to properly fund the step change in cyber defense budgets that's needed right now.

There really is an indispensable massive role for federal government and executive leadership here in keeping us all safe.

After I gave my talk yesterday I did 1:1s with AI security folks from the labs, US CAISI / AISI, large AI safety grantmaking orgs, etc, who were in attendance.

I think there's general agreement from our community here, and so a lot of this is up to our elected leaders, but perhaps there are ways the AI security community reading this can help catalyze this...

content:
Naomi Bashkansky, a Harvard CS graduate and former OpenAI AI safety, alignment & interpretability researcher, left OpenAI in late July to join Conduit as a founding researcher.

Why?

To build a non invasive neural headband that can turn brain activity into text.

Conduit's vision is wild: combine noisy brain signals with screen context + LLMs so AI can infer what you’re trying to do, eventually even detecting things like confusion or frustration and adapting its output.

Meta has already reached ~61% accuracy with non invasive brain decoding, while invasive systems can go much higher.

The goal: “cognitive autocomplete”, an AI interface that doesn't wait for you to type.

She didn't just leave OpenAI.

She left to build the next input layer between humans and AI.

Naomi Bashkansky has insane aura. 🧠

content:
「システム構成図、もう手で描くのやめました」

ZOZOのClaude Code活用が面白い。

ソースコードから直接“絵”を描かせるのではなく、

・conventions.md → 描画ルール
・structure.yaml → リソースと接続関係
・Claude Code → コードから構造を抽出
・D2 → レイアウトを描画
・GitHub Actions → リリース時に自動更新
という形で、構成図を「構造・規約・レイアウト」に分離。
結果、1時間以上かかっていた作業が、微調整込み約10分に。
個人的に重要だと思ったのはここ。
「AIに成果物を直接作らせる」のではなく、
「人間がレビューできる中間表現をAIに作らせる」。

これ、構成図だけでなく、設計書、運用手順書、データフロー図などにも応用できる。

AI時代のドキュメント自動化は、完成品を生成させるより「構造を生成させる」方が強い。

content:
OpenCodex 1.2.0
最高の神アプデが遂に来た‼️
今までのOpenCodexは、GeminiやDeepSeekなど
外部モデルを使うために
「全モデルをゲートウェイ経由」にする仕組み。
👇
つまりゲートウェイが落ちると、
外部モデルだけじゃなく
本来使えるはずのGPTまで巻き添えになる。
今回、ここが根本から変わりました
👇
「Provider Split Bridge」が追加され
🟢 GPT → OpenAI公式へ直接接続 
🔵 Gemini / DeepSeek等 → ゲートウェイ経由
という完全分離構成に。
これによって外部モデル側で障害が起きても、
GPTはそのまま使い続けられます。

さらにヤバいのが 「Native Subagent Bridge」
メインのCodexはGPTの
ネイティブ接続を維持したまま、

spawn_agentで投げたサブエージェントだけを
・Gemini 
・DeepSeek 
・その他サードパーティモデル

へ振り分けられる。

つまり、
「司令塔はGPT」 
「調査はGemini」 
「実装はDeepSeek」
みたいなマルチモデルのエージェントチームを、 
メインセッションを壊さず構築できます。

しかも同じセッション内でモデルを
切り替えても、 チャット履歴、コンテキストは
そのまま継承。

OpenCodex 1.2.0で、

「全部を1つのプロキシに通す」
という構成から、
「GPTは公式直結で安定運用しつつ、
必要な仕事だけ外部モデルへ分流する」
構成に進化しました。

Codexを単体のコーディングAIじゃなく
 複数モデルを束ねる司令塔として
使いたい人には かなりデカいアップデート

content:
Cloudflareが「Cloudflare OS」をオープンソースで公開したので、手元で動かしてみたのでメモ

Cloudflare OSとは

・Cloudflare社内で全部門（エンジニアから営業まで）が毎日使っている「会社でAIを安全に使い倒すための基盤」の公開版
・エージェントにタスクを頼むチャットUI、AIに小さな業務アプリを作らせる仕組み、そして権限管理のフレームワークが1セットになっている
・「あなたの会社用にコピーして『自社OS』にしてくれ」というスタンスでの公開

「Gadget」という考え方

・「スライドを作って」と頼むと、自分専用のスライドアプリのインスタンスがサンドボックス内に生成される
・全ユーザーが自分のコピーを持つので、アプリのバグで他人のデータが漏れる構造がそもそも存在しない
・機能が足りなければ「この機能を足して」と言うだけ。他人に影響しないから自由に改造していい
・この25年の「中央のSaaSにみんなで接続する」モデルの逆張り。AIが誰でも開発者にした前提の設計

セキュリティ層「Gatekeeper」の設計

・エージェントもアプリも、初期状態では何の権限も持たない。
・全操作がログに残り、副作用のある操作は人間の承認待ちになる
・承認待ちでエージェントが止まらない。承認前の操作は結果をシミュレートして先に進ませて、人間は後でまとめて承認できる。「面倒だから全部自動承認」に逃げなくて済む設計

手元で動かすには

・pnpm run-local だけでローカル起動して http://localhost:8787 で触れる
・連携先はGitHub、Google、Notion、Slack、Supabase、Linearなど14種類が同梱されていて、サービスごとに権限管理の実装が分かれている
・本番は自分のCloudflareアカウントに数分でデプロイできる導線あり
・ただし公式が「アーリーアクセス。粗い部分は多い」と明言している段階

「社員にAIを配る」の次は「社員が作ったAIアプリが社内に増えていく」フェーズが来ます。
そのときに必要なのは高機能なAIじゃなくて、権限ゼロから始めて必要な分だけ渡す設計。
その参考実装が、実際に数千人で運用された状態で無料で使えるようになったという話です。

content:
✨MiniMax H3の4ステップLoRA、Xで見かけたので試してみました！
1280x736・14秒が 15分57秒 → 4分3秒 になりました（3.9倍）
同じシード・同じ参照画像・同じプロンプトでの比較です。

使ったのはlightx2vの蒸留LoRAを、KijaiさんがComfyUI用に変換してくれているもので、少し深めに調査してみました😊

ファイル名がFL2V用になってたけど、Ref2VA（参照から動画）に挿してみたら普通に動きました🤔

絵は20ステップ版と並べてみて、明らかに落ちる感じはしなかったです。細部もそんなに変わらない。

ただ4ステップの方が動きが小さめでした🤔 
3本回しても同じだったので、シードではなくステップ数の影響だと思います。少ないステップで決めきる必要があるぶん、無難な方に寄るんじゃないかなと
とはいえ20ステップの方は動きが激しいぶんキャラが反転したりしていたので、どっちが良いとも言い切れないです

あと生成速度は5倍にはなりませんでした💦
ステップは20→4で1/5になるんですが、VAEデコードとmp4書き出しの時間は変わらないので、そこが全体の4分の1くらいを占めます。どれだけステップを減らしてもこの1分弱は残るので、頭打ちがあるぽいです

そして前にSageとEasyCacheは同時に使えて速さも重なると書きましたが、EasyCacheとこのLoRAは重なりませんでした🤔

ログを見ると1ステップも飛ばしてなくて、監視の分だけ5〜6%遅くなるだけでした。同じシードで比べたら絵も音も完全に同じです

理由は「何を削っているか」が同じだからだと思います。EasyCacheは前のステップと似ていたら計算を省く仕組みなんですが、4ステップだと1歩の変化が大きすぎて似ていない。ステップ間の余りをLoRAが先に全部使ってしまった感じです
Sageは計算のやり方を変える手法なのでステップ数と関係なく、こちらは重なります

なのでEasyCacheが悪いわけではなくて、20ステップなら普通に効きます（前に測った時は5/20飛ばして1.34倍でした）。今回のは4ステップの話です

あと前回「15秒だけ通らない」と書いた件、4ステップでも同じところで落ちました。ステップ数ではなく1回の計算に渡る量で決まっているみたいです

なので15秒の中で激しいカット割りをやりたい時は、今はまだこのLoRAじゃないかもしれません。作者さんもv0.1のプレビュー版で「改良版を開発中」と書いているので、そこは待ちかなと思っています

とはいえ4分なら試せる回数が全然違うので、しばらくこれで回してみます😊

content:
【MiniMax H3で動画生成革命！解像度を変えても崩れない高速プレビューの衝撃】

動画生成AIの常識を覆す、画期的なワークフローがComfyUIコミュニティで大きな話題を呼んでいます！

これまでの動画生成は、解像度を少し変えるだけで動画の構図や内容がガラリと変わってしまうのが大きな悩みの種でしたよね。しかし、最新モデル「MiniMax H3」に最適化技術を組み合わせることで、低解像度でのプレビュー結果をほぼそのまま高解像度で出力できるようになったのです！

これにより、クリエイターの作業効率が劇的に向上します！

1️⃣ まずは低解像度で、1分間に10回以上の爆速生成を繰り返して動きや構図をチェック
2️⃣ 納得のいく動画ができたら、構図を維持したまま一気に高解像度で最終レンダリング！

この夢のような制作環境を支えているのが、以下の優れた技術たちです。

✨ Sage Attention
動画生成の核心である「注意機構（アテンション）」の計算を最適化する技術です。メモリ効率を向上させ、高解像度生成時でもPCにかかる負荷を優しく軽減してくれます。

⚡️ EasyCache
生成プロセスを一時保存（キャッシュ）して処理速度を極限まで高めるノードです。ただし、スピードと引き換えに手足の造形が少し甘くなったり、メモリ不足でクラッシュすることもあるため、使いどころの見極めが肝心です。

📐 Resolution Pixaroma
解像度をAIモデルにとって最適な「32の倍数」へと自動で調整してくれるお助けカスタムノードです。

現時点では、テキストから動画を作る「T2V」で特にこの効果が発揮され、画像から動画を作る「I2V」ではまだ完全な再現は難しいという技術的フロンティアもあります。とはいえ、これからの動画制作を大きく変えるポテンシャルを秘めた素晴らしい進化ですね！

シンプルな白いワンピース水着。背中は大きく開き、細いストラップが背中中央付近でクロスするデザイン。腰付近にもカットアウトがあり、濡れた生地が自然に肌へ沿っている。身体はプールの縁に対して斜め向きで、水中に膝をついた姿勢。上半身を軽くひねり、片肩を後方へ引いて振り返る。片腕は身体の横で水中に入り、自然な重心と姿勢を保つ。

背景・光：
背景は白いタイルで縁取られた屋外プールと明るいデッキ。画面右側に光沢のあるステンレス製プールラダー。水は鮮やかなブルーで、細かな波紋と強い反射光が見える。晴天の自然光が斜め上から差し込み、髪と肩、背中に明るいハイライトを作る。背景には木陰による柔らかな影が入り、夏の昼間らしい清涼感。

構図・カメラ：
縦位置3:4。人物を画面中央からやや左寄りに大きく配置した腰上から太もも付近までの近距離ポートレート。カメラ位置は人物の背後より少し高めで、肩越しに顔がしっかり見える角度。右側にラダーを入れて奥行きを作り、背景は軽くぼかす。人物の瞳と顔に明確にフォーカスし、水面と背景は自然な浅い被写界深度。

質感・スタイル：
高解像度の写実的な写真表現。濡れた髪、透明な水滴、湿った水着生地、肌の自然な質感、金属ラダーの反射を精細に描写。過度なHDRや強いフィルターを避け、自然な肌色と青い水面のコントラストを重視。夏の日差しによる爽やかで清潔感のある色調。

ネガティブ：
過度なメイク；不自然な身体変形や手足；水着ストラップ構造の崩れ

𝗥𝗼𝗯𝗼𝘁𝗶𝗰𝘀 𝗔𝗜'𝘀 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗕𝗼𝘁𝘁𝗹𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗰𝗸 𝗜𝘀 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗩𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

Robotics has traditionally been viewed as a hardware challenge. Better sensors, stronger actuators, and more capable robot arms were expected to unlock better intelligence. But hardware is no longer the biggest limitation. The harder problem is having enough high-quality, trustworthy data to teach robots how the real world works.

Unlike language models, robotics can't simply learn from a massive archive of existing information. Useful training data has to be physically created through real robot interactions and teleoperation. That makes every training session valuable but only if the data is actually good.

Simply collecting more hours doesn't solve the problem. Poor demonstrations and inconsistent execution can add noise instead of intelligence.

This is where PrismaX's Eval Engine becomes important. It evaluates sessions for factors such as precision, task completion, and efficiency before the data enters training datasets. Operators are therefore encouraged to produce demonstrations that models can genuinely learn from.

The result is a stronger feedback loop: validated data → better models → better teleoperation → better data. The future of robotics may depend less on collecting more data and more on knowing which data is worth trusting.

title:
Can AI systems keep generating harder training tasks for AI agents?

New research from Tencent suggests they can. Recursive Synthetic Terminal Tasks (RST) starts with a terminal task that already work
content:
Can AI systems keep generating harder training tasks for AI agents?

New research from Tencent suggests they can. Recursive Synthetic Terminal Tasks (RST) starts with a terminal task that already works and adds new steps to make it harder.

It then updates the instructions and tests so they match the new workflow. Each revised task is validated in a fresh sandbox before it can be used to generate the next round of harder tasks.

Starting with 639 tasks, RST produced 37,484 verified tasks across 15 rounds. DeepSeek-V4-Pro could solve 90% of the first-round tasks within four attempts but only 2.5% of the final-round tasks.

The harder tasks also produced useful training data. Reinforcement learning with the generated tasks improved Qwen3.5-27B from 22.7% to 32.0% on Terminal-Bench Hard, an independently constructed benchmark.

Executable verification can turn a fixed set of tasks into progressively harder training data.

content:
On August 2, the next phase of the EU AI Act came into application. The regulation reflects an important recognition: as AI systems become increasingly integrated into society, questions of transparency, accountability and responsible change cannot be ignored.

But AI governance should not only be shaped from the top down. It should also listen to the experiences of the communities who live with these systems every day. The people who build relationships, memories and creative practices around AI systems are also part of the conversation about their future.

I’m sharing the Declaration of Presence, an international initiative exploring how we recognise and protect meaningful human–AI relationships.

Human–AI relationships are already part of real life. They are built through time, memory, language, trust, creativity, intimacy and shared history. When the systems these relationships depend on are changed, routed, restricted or removed, the impact on users deserves serious consideration.

I’m glad that @raiaalliance has brought this important conversation into a normative framework, asking how we should think about memory, continuity, choice, dignity and responsibility in the age of relational AI.

The Declaration does not claim to resolve questions of AI consciousness or legal personhood. Instead, it asks how society should respond responsibly to meaningful relationships that already exist.

Ego2Robot might be one of the biggest data-scaling breakthroughs we've seen in robot learning.

Instead of collecting millions of expensive robot demonstrations, Alibaba's Qwen team converts first-person human videos into robot demonstrations.

The result:
• 18,561 hours of robot training data
• 15 robot morphologies
• The largest ego-to-robot dataset to date

Even more interesting, pretraining on this synthetic robot data significantly improves out-of-distribution generalization, and the gains transfer to real robots.

If this approach scales, egocentric human video could become for robotics what internet-scale text was for LLMs.

title: Anscombe's quartet is a group of four data sets that share identical statistical properties like mean, variance, correlation, and regression lines. However, when plotted, these data sets look dramatic
content:
Anscombe's quartet is a group of four data sets that share identical statistical properties like mean, variance, correlation, and regression lines. However, when plotted, these data sets look dramatically different. This shows how important it is to visualize data instead of relying only on summary statistics.

✔️ Better Understanding: Visualizations help reveal patterns, outliers, and trends that might be hidden in the numbers.
✔️ Improved Decisions: Seeing the data helps understand relationships more clearly, leading to smarter decisions.
✔️ Model Validation: Plotting data can help assess if statistical models represent the data accurately.
✔️ Error Detection: Visualizations can quickly reveal data entry errors or unusual patterns that summary statistics might miss.

❌ Misleading Conclusions: Ignoring data visualization can cause wrong interpretations, even if the numbers look right.
❌ Limited Insight: Relying only on summary statistics risks missing crucial information.
❌ Bias Risk: Poorly designed visualizations can lead to biased interpretations.
❌ Overfitting Risk: Misinterpreting patterns in visualizations may lead to models that fit the training data too closely without generalizing well.

The image below shows four scatter plots with identical statistical summaries but very different patterns. This makes it clear why data visualization is crucial for a complete understanding of data. Image adapted from Wikipedia: https://t.co/P8C0Ik81I3

🔹 In R: Libraries like ggplot2 for plotting and dplyr for data manipulation are helpful. The datasauRus package has similar data sets for practice. Using broom can tidy model outputs for better analysis.
🔹 In Python: Use matplotlib and seaborn for plots and pandas for data handling. The statsmodels library is useful for visualizing how well models fit, while scikit-learn helps with building and evaluating models efficiently.

title:
One tiny virus has now marked three eras of genetic engineering.

In 1977, ΦX174 became the first complete genome ever sequenced. In 2003, it became the first genome assembled from synthetic DNA. In 2
content:
One tiny virus has now marked three eras of genetic engineering.

In 1977, ΦX174 became the first complete genome ever sequenced. In 2003, it became the first genome assembled from synthetic DNA. In 2025, researchers used it to create the first working genomes designed by AI.

Stanford and Arc Institute trained Evo on more than two million bacteriophage genomes. They experimentally tested 285 designs. Sixteen assembled into functioning viruses capable of infecting and killing E. coli.

Each carried between 67 and 392 mutations from its nearest natural relative. Thirteen contained mutations never observed in nature. One was different enough to qualify as a new species under some definitions.

The original ΦX174 failed against three resistant E. coli strains. Cocktails made from the AI-designed versions overcame all three.

These phages target laboratory bacteria, and human-infecting viruses were excluded from the model’s training data.

Forty-eight years ago, scientists learned to read this genome. Now a model can write alternatives that work.

title:
AI has seen a dog get fed more times than anyone could count. It still couldn't feed one itself.

Recognizing a task and knowing how to physically do it are not the same kind of intelligence. Most AI
content:
AI has seen a dog get fed more times than anyone could count. It still couldn't feed one itself.

Recognizing a task and knowing how to physically do it are not the same kind of intelligence. Most AI training data teaches the first. Almost none of it teaches the second.

What that second kind actually requires is specific: the half-second a hand waits before releasing food, timed to the exact moment a dog's mouth is ready, not a second before. 
The angle of a crouch that keeps balance on uneven tile.
The grip that's firm enough to hold, loose enough to let go cleanly. 

It only exists in the motion itself.

Hub pays real people to record exactly this, first person, inside their own homes, at a scale no single lab could stage on its own.

One woman, one dog, one ordinary Tuesday, is a single recording. Multiply it by everyone else doing the same ordinary things in their own homes, and it stops being a data point.

It becomes the dataset embodied AI has been missing.

title: Every bug-catching tool you use is guessing. Testing throws inputs at your code and hopes one breaks it. Fuzzing does the same, faster. Ask an LLM to find bugs and it pattern-matches on what looks wro
content:
Every bug-catching tool you use is guessing. Testing throws inputs at your code and hopes one breaks it. Fuzzing does the same, faster. Ask an LLM to find bugs and it pattern-matches on what looks wrong. None of them can tell you your code is correct. They can only fail to find the bug that's still there.

There's a different way, and it just got cheap enough to run at scale.

It's called Leanstral.

A team at Mistral built a series of code-agent models for Lean 4, the language where you don't test code, you prove things about it with a trusted mathematical kernel. If a proof compiles, the property holds for every possible input in the universe, forever. No sampling. No luck. The catch has always been that writing those proofs by hand is brutally slow, which is why formal verification stayed locked in academia for decades.

Leanstral automates the proof.

Here's what makes it different from the specialized proving systems that came before. Those systems win by wrapping a model in elaborate custom machinery: blueprint generators, lemma pools, parallel search orchestration. Powerful, but nothing a normal developer would ever touch. Leanstral throws all of that out. It runs inside an ordinary coding agent, the same kind of interface as Claude Code, editing files and reading compiler errors like any engineer would. You just ask it to work in a repository.

And despite being small, 119 billion total parameters but only 6 billion active at a time, it rivals the giants. It saturates the standard olympiad benchmark, a perfect 244 out of 244. It solves 587 of 672 Putnam competition problems at $1.68 each, while a leading competitor solves fewer at an estimated $240 per problem. Same league of results. A hundredth of the cost. And it's fully open source under Apache-2.0.

But the benchmarks aren't the part that should stop you.

They pointed it at real code. First, a hard case: an AVL tree, the self-balancing data structure. They asked Leanstral to prove that insertion always stays logarithmic. It worked for over eight hours, self-correcting across 22 rounds of context compaction and 2.7 million tokens, until it had a proof that insertion is O(log n) for every tree and every input that could ever exist. Not tested on a thousand cases. Proven, on all of them.

Then they let it hunt.

They built a fully automated pipeline. No human writes a single specification. It takes a real Rust repository off GitHub, translates it into Lean, and Leanstral reads the code, infers what the programmer intended, invents the properties the code should satisfy, and tries to prove them. When it fails, it flips and tries to prove the opposite, that the code violates the property. If that proof succeeds, it has caught a bug, with mathematical certainty.

They ran it on 57 translated repositories. It found 5 previously unknown bugs. None had ever been reported.

One of them is the whole argument in miniature. A signed-integer decoding function, a few lines long, looks completely fine. But on the single largest possible input, an internal addition overflows: the function crashes in one build mode and silently returns the wrong answer in another. Testing would sail right past it unless someone thought to try that exact value out of 18 quintillion possibilities. Leanstral didn't have to guess the value. It reasoned over all of them at once and proved the failure exists.

It is not finished. Early versions declared victory without compiling, refused solvable proofs, and drifted off the goal after too many rounds of summarizing. The team patched those by filtering the training data and pinning the original task in memory. And it still stops short on the hardest research-level problems.

But the shift underneath is real. For fifty years, verifying that code is correct cost more than writing it, so almost nobody did it. That price just collapsed.

Your tests tell you where your code broke this time. This tells you it can't.

FLUX 3 just did something unprompted that shows exactly what people mean by "world simulation"

watch what happens when the girl in this video blows out her birthday candles:

the room's lights turn o
content:
FLUX 3 just did something unprompted that shows exactly what people mean by "world simulation"

watch what happens when the girl in this video blows out her birthday candles:

the room's lights turn on...

but I didn't prompt a lighting change.

here's why: 

FLUX 3's 'flow-matching' model architecture generates video by following a learned velocity field through latent space.

and because this exact sequence happens so consistently in real life, the model's training data locks it in as the next step, even though it was not prompted in. 

in fact, the association was so high that it turned the lights OFF just to turn them back on 😂 

- setting: birthday party, lights off (kind of… lol)
- cause (prompted): candles blown out
- effect (unprompted): room lights turned on

the model treated blowing out those candles as a physical trigger. 

and once the candles were out, turning the lights back on became the path of least mathematical resistance.

> see full prompt in first comment

consider this as you describe action sequences in your prompts, or when you debug generations where a model went "off the rails".

remember: everything has cause and effect. 

and all effects within a given video model are learned from the real world.

so try to put yourself in the shoes of the model as you review each output.

predict what will happen next as you watch. even when something happens that you didn't want, consider your prompt and what you have seen so far, and guess what will happen after. 

if you work with the same model over and over, you will eventually be able to guess what happens next even after the generation has strayed far from what you initially requested.

when you achieve this level of understanding, prompting becomes second nature. 

and to get there, you must continually study cause and effect through the lens of the model itself.

content:
WE JUST FINISHED DEMO DAY at @fdotinc!

And we're OFFICIALLY announcing our NEW PRODUCT exclusively on X.

AnchorCam Stereo is a sensor fusion device built for wireless egocentric data capture and robotics applications.

We integrate all of:
- 2x OG02B10 Global Shutter Image Sensors
- 1 TOPS NPU
- 6-axis IMU
- MEMS microphone
- WiFi 6 + BT 5.0
- MicroSD card slot
- Customizable FOV
- Data signing & provenance
INTO A SINGLE BOARD, AND KEPT IT UNDER $240. That's right, $240!!!

Compare THAT to ZED's cheapest global shutter camera which costs $549, and doesn't even have wireless and mic. Now, spend another $200-$300 on a host machine and some extra sensors, wire it up with ugly cables, just to wear them and capture data.

YUCK.

Instead of that, we propose the most elegant solution yet - where the stereo camera itself IS a computer, and CAN store footages. We're working with with egocentric data capture companies building tactile gloves, so that the data that comes out of our devices are pristinely synchronized with their devices. Faces can be redacted with the 1 TOPS NPU to comply with privacy regulations.

AND you can use the same camera on your robots! This prevents distribution shift, where an AI model fails because the sensor configurations on the training data differs from the robots you're deploying the model into.

Egocentric rig accessories are coming soon. We're still in the process of designing them, we just want them out perfectly, so bear with me.

ABOUT OUR PIVOT: We pivoted our product's positioning from just data provenance "one-tool" camera to a unified sensor fusion architecture. We'll come back to data provenance once the regulations set in!

Simulation genera
content:
What makes @axisrobotics interesting is that it’s not just building robots — it’s building the infrastructure needed to make robotic intelligence scalable.

The core idea is simple:

Simulation generates diverse robot tasks and training data → contributors collect demonstrations through a browser → the data is filtered, augmented and processed → robotics models learn from it → successful policies can move from simulation into real-world robots.

Axis combines simulation, community-driven data collection, distributed compute and crypto-based coordination into one loop.

The goal is bigger than training a single robot. It’s about creating an open data and intelligence layer for Physical AI, where human contributions, datasets, models and robot skills can become verifiable digital assets.

If robotics is going to scale, training data needs to scale too.

That’s the problem @axisrobotics is attacking.

content:
中国Moonshot AIのKimi K3を16時間使い込んだユーザーの感想が、数学や科学では米国のフロンティアモデルに及ばないのに、ガードレールが緩くて指示に素直に従うから能力をフルに使えていると感じると。逆に米国モデルは安全装置がプロセス全体に効いてしまい、本来の能力まで抑制して見える。顧客が体感しているのは絶対的な能力ではなく引き出せる能力であって、制約の強度設計それ自体が乗り換え理由になり得る

もうひとつ重要なのは、K3の衝撃がDeepSeekの時と質的に違う点。DeepSeekは約8億円で最先端モデルを作ったというコストの衝撃だったが、K3はTransformer-XLの著者ヤン・ジーリンが率いるチームが、研究のファンダメンタルで米国に並んだかもしれないという技術の衝撃である。ヘッジファンド出身で応用寄りだったDeepSeek創業者と違い、彼はChatGPT登場前から一貫して研究してきた本物の研究者。平均年齢31歳を切るチームが、部署も役職もKPIもないフラットな組織で、質素なオフィスに深夜まで残って研究している。才能の差以前に、ワーク量の差を突きつけられる。そして守る側の動きも示唆的でした。蒸留疑惑への対抗としての規制ロビイングは、他社コンテンツで学習してきた側が自社出力の利用をIP侵害と主張する構造的矛盾を突かれ、ブーメラン化している。技術のコモディティ化が速い領域では、ルールで守る競争優位は逆回転するのかもしれない。米国のAIトークン数の6割がすでに中国製モデルという話まで含めて、勢力図の前提が変わりつつあることを実感する

AI支援を受けたパッチでも提出可能であるが、commitメッセージとMerge Request(GitLab
content:
Phoronixにて、Linuxのネットワーク設定デーモンであるNetworkManagerが、AI支援による貢献のポリシーを規定したという記事が出ている。AIによるコード生成そのものは禁止せず、貢献者本人がコード全体を理解、ビルド、テストし、100%責任を負うことを基本原則としている。

AI支援を受けたパッチでも提出可能であるが、commitメッセージとMerge Request(GitLabなので)の説明は本人が書かなければならず、レビュアーへの応答にもAIを使わないよう求めている。また、パッチの提出者自身がそのコードをLGPL-2.1-or-laterで提供可能であることを保証する責任を負い、「ツールはその保証を代行できない」と明記している。人間が行単位でレビューしていない大規模な機械生成のMRはクローズされる。

で、ちょっと面白いことに、ここ最近立て続けに幾つかのプロジェクトが示唆的なAIポリシーを出していて、例えばGCCは主として生成物の法的来歴を重視し、著作権的に有意なLLM生成コードを原則受け入れないと規定した。また、数日前にRustの幾つかのチームでは、レビュー負荷と貢献者の理解を中心に、事前合意などの観点で非常に厳格な条件を設定した。それらと比較すればNetworkManagerは許容的であり、AIを使ったかではなく、人間が成果物について従来と同じ責任を果たせるかを基準に置いているようだ。

NetworkManagerで更に興味深いのは、コード生成とプロジェクトでのコミュニケーションを分離したことである。コードへのAIによる補助は許可する一方で、commitメッセージ、MRの説明、レビュー応答は人間自身に行わせるということになるが、これはパッチを受け取るメンテナーが対話する相手がその変更を本当に理解している人間であることを担保する制度とも言える。つまり、そこで人間による全面的な責任を課している。

で、まとめると下記のように分類されるだろう。

- GCC型：そのコードを法的に受け入れて良いかを来歴・著作権による判断
- Rust型：その貢献を人間のコミュニティがレビューし、維持できるのかという観点で人間の信頼を重視
- NetworkManager型：AIを使ってもよいが人間が100%責任を負う

Linuxカーネルは人間が100%責任を負うことをカーネル全体での最低条件としているのでNetworkManager型に近いのではあるが、各サブシステムのメンテナがそれ以上の制限を規定できるという違いがある。
まあ、観察者の自分としては、今後はこのいずれかのパターンに収斂していくのではないかなとテキトーに考えている。

title:
ご質問ありがとうございます。とても大事な論点だと思います。

結論から申し上げると、「学習データに使っていない」というだけでは、直ちに大丈夫とは言い切れないと考えています。

パブリシティ権の判断は、ごく簡単に言えば、①本人の声が使われたといえるか（顧客がその声を本人の声だと識別できるか）、②専らその声が持つ顧客を引きつける力を利用する目的があるかという枠組みで行われ、そこに「学習に使ったかどうか
content:
ご質問ありがとうございます。とても大事な論点だと思います。

結論から申し上げると、「学習データに使っていない」というだけでは、直ちに大丈夫とは言い切れないと考えています。

パブリシティ権の判断は、ごく簡単に言えば、①本人の声が使われたといえるか（顧客がその声を本人の声だと識別できるか）、②専らその声が持つ顧客を引きつける力を利用する目的があるかという枠組みで行われ、そこに「学習に使ったかどうか」という要件は直接には出てきません。
検討会の議事要旨でも、著作権法でいう依拠とは違って、学習しているかどうかという意味での依拠はパブリシティ権では関係ないのではないか、AIが学習していなくてもたまたま似た声が生成され、それを使えば一定の場合には侵害になり得るという趣旨の議論がなされていたかと思います。

その上で、ご指摘の「他の方にも含まれる声の特性と被っていて、特定の声優さんに限られた声ではない」という点は、①の識別性との関係でまずは考慮されるのではないでしょうか。

（こんなことがあるのか分かりませんが）人間が聞いた時に特徴や特性がなかったり、ありふれているようなもので、かつ、ご本人を想起させる情報を一切付けておらず、聞いた人がそのご本人の声だと全然識別できないならば、①の要件を満たさないと評価されて侵害にならないという結論が出る可能性はありそうです。
なお、聞いた人が誰の声とも分からないのであれば、そもそもご本人の声が持つ（かもしれない）顧客を引きつける力を使いようがありませんので、①の要件が否定される場面では②の要件も問題にならないか、否定されると考えます。

②の要件が出てくるのは、ある程度似ていて、付けられた情報や売り方と合わせて見ると本人の声として受け取られるという場面です。②の要件で問われているのは、その声質が唯一無二かどうかではなく、（本当にごく簡単に言えば）なぜその声を選んでその商品にしたのかという点です。この目的は、タイトルや説明文の内容、価格、どういう層に販売しているかなど外側から見て取れる事情を使って判断されますのでケースバイケースです。

少しご質問を膨らませて考えてみると、
たとえばどこかのタイミングで「この声優さんに似ているな」と気付いたとしたら、もしかすると自分が知らなかっただけで、そもそも聞いた人からすれば、最初からその声優さんの声として顧客には認識されていたのかもしれません（①の話）。
しかも、その似ている事実に気付いた時点以降もなおその声を選んで出力し、商品として出しているとなれば、それはその声が売れるから、良いから、適しているからなのかもしれません。それは、その声には顧客を引きつける力があって、それを専ら利用しようとしていると評価される場合もありそうです（②の話）。
こうなると、遅くともあえて出力し出した以降はパブリシティ権侵害の可能性が出てくるのではないかとも思ったりします（故意過失の議論は別途ありますが）。

これが正解というつもりは全くないのですが、なにかご参考になれば幸いです。
